body:
Potential reference implementation: https://github.com/denysdovhan/spaceship-prompt/blob/master/sections/elixir.zsh

@ntilotta I don't know anything about Elixir, and the only thing I know about Erlang was a failed attempt to learn it in undergrad that nearly broke my brain. Do the two languages interact at all, or are they separate like Java/Scala?

@chipbuster they are two different languages but they can interact each other, if I can suggest the best way should be supporting Elixir and its package manager Hex (https://hex.pm/) so in this case it should be able to support Erlang too, the languages runs in the same VM and you can use the same package manager for both.

Anyway I think supporting Elixir will be enough, it provides a better toolchain than Erlang so it should be easier to implement it using the reference implementation you linked upon.
Thanks for the info, and thanks for the suggestion!
I would love to help test this out when it becomes available. Please let me know if I can help.

Support for erlang and elixir would not be very hard at all.

For elixir, the output of `elixir --version` gives the erlang version (OTP), build flags, and elixir version.  The version of the project in the cwd is available in `mix.exs` in a line most commonly like `version: "0.4.3"` (though the file is code so this is not necessarily certain, but only once seen a project that didn't hardcode it here (and they had it access it via a git tag lookup each time).

Unfortunetly, the `elixir --version` call can take a full second to return, even only doing it in directories with `mix.exs` (though in directories with elixir source files would be useful) would be annoyingly slow, so the information really needs to be cached.

A popular tool in the elixir ecosystem is `asdf`, so if an `asdf` module is installed then it could pull the elixir version information from that a *LOT* faster than caling `elixir --version`.

So I did some thinking here and feel like this might be one of those modules which would slow down Starship for the reasons discussed above. As a user, I would be fine with this functionality being "off by default" since it could slow things down and then I'd be comfortable having to turn it on myself in the config. Is such a thing doable or desirable? I'm not sure how to approach this but I might be willing to help implement given some direction.

If starship used async updating, or a cache, that would fix the great majority of the speed issues.

I'm still curious about if starship were a persistent service that was called to print the line, doing everything in the background, so even on shells without async updateable prompts it could be fast but 'prepping' on the first line in a directory, but another update would then show the correct information.

>If starship used async updating

I thought about this at one point, but I don't think it's possible without a major overhaul of how shells and term emulators work (and I suspect it's just not ever going to happen e.g. for `bash`). As a standalone program that works outside the shell's internal mechanism, it's going to be one hell of a trick to do async updating in shells that don't explicitly support it.

> or a cache

This is a good idea as well, but this would only be useful for very specific things (mostly software versions on slow-launching commands). A pretty huge chunk of our stuff is already gated by file-existence checks, and caching the existence of files in a file somewhat defeats the point. Of course, this brings us to your next point...

>  if starship where a persistent service

Yes! I thought about this for a while when I first saw this project, and my conclusion is that it's eminently possible. The speed gains (e.g. by caching versions of programs and async updating them, or by caching the results of parsing a complex file and only updating it when `inotify` tells you it's changed) could be pretty big for complex directories, like the fork of LLVM that I have (which raises my prompt render time from 0.03s to 0.5s every time I `cd` into it)

Of course, we're dealing with some challenges here:
  - What should the behavior be if the service is unreachable (e.g crashed or socket disrupted?)
  - What's the communication cost? With hot caches, the render time is currently 0.01s--if we have a service that you have to `connect()` to every time (because starship isn't persistent--we have to re-establish communications on every launch), what does the render time look like?
  - How should we deal with the situation where the user doesn't have permissions to launch a persistent daemon? Do we launch a persistent daemon each time the user logs in? Each time they launch a shell? Only one for as long as user is logged in? We want starship to be usable with minimal configuration, and adding in a standalone process in the background complicates this a lot.

I really like the idea here, and it might be good for a long-lived experimental starship branch, or maybe a fork of the project. Given that the standalone-program-for-prompt-rendering paradigm is (as far as I know) still a fairly new one, I don't think we'll be able to implement this for quite a while, possibly ever.

We still have trouble testing the connector code (in `init.rs`) that ties the starship binary into the rest of the shell, and this would *not* be helped by trying to introduce a standalone info-caching process that communicates asynchronously with the shell.

In conclusion, I love the idea, but unless we get a full-time Rusteacean or two working on it, I don't see it being implemented anytime in the next year or two.

> What should the behavior be if the service is unreachable (e.g crashed or socket disrupted?)

I'd imagine what it is doing now, just processing in the request then closing down again.

> What's the communication cost? With hot caches, the render time is currently 0.01s--if we have a service that you have to connect() to every time (because starship isn't persistent--we have to re-establish communications on every launch), what does the render time look like?

If it's just a simple named pipe, pretty trivial, shouldn't raise the times by anything noticeable at all.  Even if it were more complex like a socket or TCP connection (TCP overhead on local machine is barely measurable).  Perhaps even DBUS could be very nice as you could plug in new functionality very easily then.

> How should we deal with the situation where the user doesn't have permissions to launch a persistent daemon?

I'd definitely say the daemon should be per-user, perhaps via systemd user services if on a systemd system, or just nohup'ing a background service on demand when required or so.  For something that's not systemd managed then it could even shut itself down if no requests after a period of time.

> Do we launch a persistent daemon each time the user logs in?

I'd say that should be user chosen.  I'd opt for a systemd user service.  That way it would launch when I am logged in any way at any place, and shut down when my last connection disconnects.

> Each time they launch a shell?

That could potentially be an option as well, just launch it in the background with `nohup` and have it die when it's gid dies.

> Only one for as long as user is logged in?

Lot's of choices, could also be a pluggable system.

> We want starship to be usable with minimal configuration, and adding in a standalone process in the background complicates this a lot.

By default I'd honestly opt for a systemd user service if it exists or just a background `nohup`'d daemon to a named pipe in some XDG path to test if its alive and setup a communication channel in any way (or just dbus it?).

> In conclusion, I love the idea, but unless we get a full-time Rusteacean or two working on it, I don't see it being implemented anytime in the next year or two.

I really don't see it taking that long, this is a fairly common pattern in a lot of things.  Someone could easily whip up a basic single-style example in less than an hour, which at that point it's just making out all the prompt plugins for it.

This is all how I'd implement it if I were writing for my Arch/Clear Linux box, but what if we don't have systemd or dbus, say because we're running on MacOS, Windows, Android (we just added a termux package), or Void Linux?

> Someone could easily whip up a basic single-style example in less than an hour

While I wouldn't be comfortable making this the default architecture for all starship (mostly because of support issues), you are absolutely correct in that, specifically as far as supporting just Linux goes, there's a pretty standard template. I was worried about universal support, but given that this daemon acts more like an in-memory cache than an authoritative source, we always have the option to just not use it.

Perhaps one way to implement this would be to provide a background daemon based on dbus/named pipes and systemd, specifically as an opt-in option for systems that support it (we could even drop instructions for configuring it into the `Advanced Configuration` section). As long as the communication protocol used is consistent, we could worry about adding backgrounding support for other platforms as time allowed.

EDIT: Of course, this would mean that we can't rely on caching behavior when evaluating new modules for speed :\

> This is all how I'd implement it if I were writing for my Arch/Clear Linux box, but what if we don't have systemd or dbus, say because we're running on MacOS, Windows, Android (we just added a termux package), or Void Linux?

Background processes with sockets or named pipes tend to be a good fallback method everywhere.  Though less efficient for better methods.

> While I wouldn't be comfortable making this the default architecture for all starship (mostly because of support issues),

Oh absolutely not, it would be something like a debug mode.

> I was worried about universal support, but given that this daemon acts more like an in-memory cache than an authoritative source, we always have the option to just not use it.

True that, the absolute fallback is just to run it per prompt without any backend, it is just a background processing engine is all, purely an optimization.

> Perhaps one way to implement this would be to provide a background daemon based on dbus/named pipes and systemd, specifically as an opt-in option for systems that support it (we could even drop instructions for configuring it into the Advanced Configuration section). As long as the communication protocol used is consistent, we could worry about adding backgrounding support for other platforms as time allowed.

It would be easy to expand it over time if the overall interfaces are abstract enough, which isn't hard to do for a project like this.

I absolutely love where this conversation is headed. We should definitely open an issue to further discuss how we can improve performance across the board on starship.

Bringing the conversation back to elixir specifically, could you foresee any issues with a primitive version caching mechanism that checks the "Date Created", "Last Modified", or "Filesize" of the binary being called? To me, this sounds like it could be a solid solution for just about any external binary we call, assuming it works 😛

For elixir, except for date created (which isn't really a good thing to check across OS's) those attributes (or a hash of them) should be perfectly sufficient for a simple cache, I'd imagine that would be the case for most things.
